svg.font-family: 'Noto Sans', system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Steering and judging AI output
svg.desc: How text written by a language model reads, why, and how to steer and judge it: stock names and words, confident wrong answers, typical ideas, dense and padded text, and review in a fresh session.
svg.text: Steering and judging AI output

AI text tends to sound alike, state guesses as facts, lose what made an idea distinctive and pack too much into each sentence. These habits are linked to how models are trained. Steer with what you know, and review in a fresh session.
1. How an AI agent works
2. Inside one reply
3. Trust and control
One realistic problem, from question to decision
Panels A to E show parts of it in more detail. The town and its numbers are made up.
you steer here
Ask
You describe the problem with the facts you know.
You: 14 people in our town died in last
summer's heat wave, most of them over 75
and living alone. What can we do before
next summer?
(thinking) heat plans,
cooling rooms, awareness
campaigns ...
Model: writes the
plan below.
Model: "Done. The plan is
complete and evidence-based."
The output
A plan of five sentences, with a common problem in each.
According to
Dr. Elara Voss
, a heat-safety expert, every town must act now.
Cooling rooms cut heat deaths by 80%, studies show.
The town should
raise awareness, plant more trees and launch an app
Meanwhile,
isolation-driven heat-risk clustering outruns our outreach
In conclusion, protecting residents from heat matters because everyone deserves to be safe.
you steer here
Review
The same output and the same request, in two sessions.
In the same session
set-up
you: what can we do before next summer?
the plan
"Done. The plan is complete and evidence-based."
you: review this plan for the town council
"Looks good: complete and evidence-based."
In a fresh session
set-up
you: review this plan for the town council
the plan, and nothing else
no reasoning and no claims
from the writer
"Five problems, from the invented expert to the padding."
Starts from the writer's own claims, and here it misses all five
problems.
Gets only what a council member gets, and here it finds all five.
Both results are made up to show the difference.
you steer here
Ask again
You send back what the review found, with the tips from panels B, C and D.
You: Leave out the expert and the 80%, unless you can
quote a source. Give five ideas, with how likely each one
is. Write in plain words for the council.
Model: five ideas, each with how likely it is
an awareness campaign
plant more trees
a heat-warning app
volunteers phone people over 75
you keep it
free buses to cooling rooms
you keep it
The two unlikely ideas reach the people who live alone, so you keep them.
you steer here
Decide
Add facts that are not in the training text or the conversation, check every claim, and choose.
Most of last summer's deaths were people over 75 who lived alone, many in top-floor flats.
Volunteers will phone every registered resident over 75 on heat-warning days, and visit anyone who does not answer.
The library and two schools will open as cooling rooms until 9 pm, with free buses from the tower blocks.
You add who died and where they lived, and which buildings can open. Residents and the care service review the plan before the council votes.
Where these habits come from
Simplified: three kinds of training, and the habits linked to each one.
Learning from a huge amount of text
The model learns which words usually follow
which, from text collected up to a cutoff date.
Heat waves are most dangerous for ...
older people
children
pets
The longer the bar, the more often that word
came next in the text.
Facts seen only once, and events after the
cutoff, get guessed. B [4, 5]
Training on human ratings
People, or models trained on their choices,
score answers.
"Great question! ... I hope this helps!"
picked
"Open the cooling rooms."
The model learns to write more like the picked
answer.
Familiar text scores well: stock names,
typical ideas. A, C [2, 8]
Agreeing and longer answers score well.
Training and tests with checkable
answers
Math, code and quiz questions, where a
program marks each answer right or wrong.
right answer: 1 point
wrong answer: 0 points
"I don't know": 0 points
A guess scores better than "I don't know".
Short solutions win, and text may get
dense. D [9]
Words used here
Model: the neural network that reads text and images and writes
text, for example Claude Opus, GPT or Gemini. Open-weight
models such as Qwen or DeepSeek can also run on your own
computer.
Harness: the program around the model. It builds the context
window, sends it to the model, runs the tools and asks for your
permission. For example Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI,
Cursor, Pi or OpenCode.
Session: one conversation with its own context window. A new
session starts with an empty conversation.
Training: how a model is built, from text collected up to a cutoff
date. The model does not change while you use it.
Training on human ratings: a late step in training, where people,
or models trained on their choices, score answers. The model
learns to write the answers that score well.
The same few names and words
A
Stock names in some 2025 model versions
GPT
Elara Voss
Claude
Elena Vasquez, Marcus Chen, Amara Okafor
Gemini
Aris Thorne, Lena Petrova
In 20,000 stories from four models
88.3% contain at least one of 11 words, such as
Elias
Mara
Elara
lighthouse
clockmaker
librarian
Ask for a story, an example or an expert, and models pick from a
short list of names, places and jobs. [1, 2]
Each model version has its own names, and newer versions use
them less, so the names also show roughly when a text was
written. [1]
One study found 1,655 fake research records with real DOIs
(permanent research identifiers). Their most frequent author,
Elena Vasquez (77 records), is a Claude stock name. [1]
Some words became far more common in scientific abstracts,
likely because scientists used AI: "delve", "intricate" and
"underscore". [3]
Why: in OLMo, the only model in the study with public
training data, these story words are rare in books and web
text. They are more frequent in the data of each later
training step, but still too rare to explain the result. [2] For
words such as "delve", a comparison of models fits training
on human ratings, but a test with human raters did not
confirm it. [3]
Tip: give real names and details yourself. A stock name in a
text is a sign that a model wrote it, so check that the person
exists.
Pulled toward the typical
C
Original idea: a heat-wave poster. A row of
balconies, everyone outside except behind
one closed curtain: "Knock on that door."
an image and a
feeling
Shortened: heat wave. Check on older
neighbours.
only the facts are left
Written again: stay safe this summer!
Remember to check on elderly neighbours
and stay hydrated in hot weather!
longer, more varied
words, no idea
The example is made up to show the finding.
In a study on advertising, models shortened creative ideas step
by step. The metaphors, emotion and images went first, and the
plain facts stayed. [6]
Written again from the short version, the text got longer and
used more varied words, but the original ideas did not come
back. It looked new without being original. [6]
Giving the model a metaphor, an emotion or an image to use
helped, but only in part. [6]
People who write with AI move toward the typical too. In a study
with 118 writers from India and the US, AI suggestions moved
the Indian writers toward Western writing styles. [7]
Why: people who rate answers tend to prefer familiar text.
Training on human ratings therefore makes typical answers
more likely, while models before this step give more varied
answers. [8]
Tip: ask for five options together with how likely each one is,
then look at the unlikely ones. In one study this made
stories, poems and jokes 1.6 to 2.1 times more varied. [8]
Confident and wrong
B
How often a fact is in the training text
many times
usually right
once
often guessed
after the cutoff date
guessed or out of date
A wrong answer reads as sure as a right one: an invented expert,
a number with no source, a function that does not exist.
If 20% of birthdays appear only once in the training text, expect
wrong answers to at least 20% of birthday questions. [4]
The training text stops at a cutoff date, for example June 2026
for current Claude models. Later events and software versions
are not in it. [5]
Why: a fact that appears only once in the training text is
often not learned, and the model writes a likely answer
instead. Tests, and the training that uses them, score "I don't
know" like a wrong answer, so a guess scores better on
average. [4]
Tip: give the model the sources and ask for quotes from
them. Check every number, name and quote yourself.
Dense inside, padded outside
D
28 words
Great question! Heat safety is an important topic, and there are
many factors to consider. In short, open the cooling rooms on
heat-warning days. I hope this helps!
7 words, same content
Open the cooling rooms on heat-warning days.
Both happen at once: padding around the answer, and dense
phrasing inside it.
isolation-driven heat-risk clustering
outruns
our outreach
stacked nouns
a thing that acts like a living being
Plainer: people who live alone are most at risk, and our outreach
does not reach them.
A 2026 study compared nine leading models with human
writing. All nine used more rare word sequences, and more
often made a thing act like a living being, as in "is_file() swallows
that". Most also used more stacked nouns. Each of these makes
the reader hold more in mind, or read the sentence again. [9]
Claude Opus 5.5 used these features less than Claude Opus 5 in
19 of 21 comparisons, clearly in 8. [9]
A long answer looks thorough, but length is not a measure of
quality.
Why: in training on human ratings, the scoring models give
longer answers higher scores. [10] In training on math and
code problems, there is pressure for short solutions. One
study suggests that this makes text dense: in its small test, a
penalty for long answers made a model's phrasing less like
human phrasing. [9]
Tip: ask for a short answer in plain words for the people who
will read it, then edit it yourself.
Review in a fresh session
E
Give the reviewer
Leave out
the task
the writer's reasoning
the output
the writer's claims
a way to check it
your opinion
A reviewer in the same session reads the writer's plan, reasoning
and claims, such as "the plan is complete and evidence-based",
and starts from them.
Some harnesses start a subagent with only the task and the
output, and it works like a fresh session. A fork starts with a copy
of the conversation, so it does not. [11]
Models score their own text higher, and the better a model
recognises its own text, the larger this bias. A fresh session of
the same model still has it. [12]
Models also tend to agree with the person asking. This is called
sycophancy. [13]
Why: people rate answers that agree with them higher, so
training on human ratings rewards agreeing. [13]
Tip: review in a fresh session, with another model or a
person [12], and keep your opinion out of the request.
A
B
C
D
E

Diagnosing Low Diversity in LLM Stories" (EMNLP 2026, arxiv.org/abs/2605.26492); [3] Juzek and Ward,

"Why Does ChatGPT 'Delve' So Much? Exploring the Sources of Lexical Overrepresentation in Large Language Models" (COLING 2025, arxiv.org/abs/2412.11385); [4] Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang, "Why Language Models Hallucinate" (2025, arxiv.org/abs/2509.04664); [5] Anthropic, "Models overview" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview); [6]

Keon et al., "Galton's Law of Mediocrity: Why Large Language Models Regress to the Mean and Fail at Creativity in Advertising" (2025, arxiv.org/abs/2509.25767); [7] Agarwal, Naaman and Vashistha, "AI Suggestions Homogenize Writing Toward Western Styles and Diminish Cultural Nuances" (CHI 2025, arxiv.org/abs/2409.11360); [8] Zhang et al., "Verbalized

Sampling: How to Mitigate Mode Collapse and Unlock LLM Diversity" (ICML 2026, arxiv.org/abs/2510.01171); [9] Clark, Martin and Mahowald, "Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?" (2026, arxiv.org/abs/2610.29162); [10] Singhal, Goyal, Xu and Durrett, "A Long Way to Go: Investigating Length Correlations in RLHF" (COLM 2024,

arxiv.org/abs/2310.03716); [11] Claude Code docs, "Create custom subagents" (code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents); [12] Panickssery, Bowman and Feng, "LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations" (2024, arxiv.org/abs/2404.13076); [13] Sharma et al., "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models" (ICLR 2024,
arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548). The town, its numbers and the example texts are made up.
